q: Does the fully-implicit parity QAOA advantage over standard unencoded QAOA survive on weighted-MaxCut or higher-order (k-body, k>=3) Ising problems, or is it specific to the paper's uniform U[-1,1] all-to-all 2-body class?
basis: This replication only tested J_ij ~ U[-1,1] on K_6, exactly as in the paper. The parity code's constraint structure is defined for pair-couplings; k-body terms require either extra ancillas or additional constraint cycles that were not touched here. Whether the ~8x E_res advantage at p=3 persists on weighted / higher-order instances is untested and non-obvious.
next_steps: Extend the numpy simulator to (a) draw J_ij from realistic weighted distributions (log-normal, portfolio-covariance-like) and (b) accept a user-supplied HZ diagonal that encodes 3- and 4-body Ising terms via additional parity ancillas. Rerun the same nr in {0.0, 0.4, 0.6, 1.0} sweep at N=6, p=3 on >=24 instances per family. Compare median E_res and fidelity to the paper's numbers and to a standard-QAOA baseline with matched circuit-depth budget. Endpoint: local CPU (Argo/CELS not needed).

q: How does parity QAOA compose with error-mitigation techniques (ZNE, PEC, symmetry verification) --- does the parity code's built-in symmetry make virtual-distillation-style verification essentially free, or does the constraint-preserving driver break the mitigation ansatz?
basis: The parity encoding provides a natural check: any measured bitstring that violates a plaquette constraint is a detected error. The paper does not test this. Standard ZNE/PEC assume a homogeneous noise model on the physical layout; the mixed explicit/implicit driver has structurally different gate footprints per nr, so mitigation gains may not be uniform.
next_steps: Build a Qiskit-Aer noise-model rerun of the same 24 instances at CNOT error rates in {1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2, 3e-2}. For each nr, compute (i) raw E_res, (ii) E_res after post-selection on satisfied constraints (symmetry verification), (iii) E_res after Richardson ZNE with noise factors [1,2,3]. Report the effective 'noise-scaling exponent' gain per nr. Free endpoint: local CPU with Aer, no Argo/CELS needed. ~2 CPU-hours.

q: On a concrete near-term optimization benchmark with limited native connectivity (a specific superconducting-qubit heavy-hex or ion-trap linear layout), does parity QAOA give a real depth advantage over SWAP-network compiled standard QAOA on the same problem?
basis: The paper's C4 claim (O(N) implicit vs O(1) explicit driver depth) is stated in terms of driver-line lengths, not compiled physical circuit depth on a specific coupling map. For portfolio-optimization or TSP instances, standard QAOA needs a SWAP network whose depth scales as O(N) on nearest-neighbor grids -- the parity encoding may or may not win once real SWAPs are counted.
next_steps: Take the paper's N=6 complete-graph Ising, plus one concrete benchmark (e.g. 6-asset Markowitz portfolio, or 6-city TSP-as-Ising). Compile (a) standard QAOA to IBM heavy-hex and IonQ linear coupling maps using Qiskit's default SABRE transpiler, (b) parity QAOA to the native LHZ square-lattice layout, and compare total 2-qubit gate count and depth per QAOA layer. Report a break-even N above which parity wins in physical depth. Free endpoint: local Qiskit transpiler runs, no hardware needed.

q: How sensitive is the parity-QAOA advantage to the constraint penalty strength c in H_C = (c/2) sum (1 - prod sigma_z), and does an adaptive scheduling c(t) or c(nr) improve both the fully-explicit and hybrid limits?
basis: This replication fixed c=3.0 (chosen to place the constraint gap comfortably above the |J_ij| scale). The paper discusses c only briefly. The fully-explicit variant's poor performance (median E_res=0.479) may be partly a consequence of a suboptimal fixed c: too small and the code space is not enforced; too large and it creates a barren-plateau-like landscape on the QAOA parameters.
next_steps: Sweep c in {0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 10.0} for nr in {0.4, 0.6, 1.0} on 12 instances at N=6, p=3. Then try an adaptive schedule c_l = c0 * (1 + l/p) that ramps c across QAOA layers (annealing-inspired). Report best median E_res per (nr, c-schedule) and compare against the fixed-c=3.0 baseline in results.json. If adaptive c closes >30% of the implicit-vs-explicit gap, the paper's ordering claim needs a caveat. Free endpoint: same numpy simulator, ~30 CPU-min per c value.

q: Does the modular (arbitrary lmax) construction of Sec. IV-V actually give a size-independent per-layer depth in practice for N in {8, 10, 12, 15}, or does the pattern-of-cycles overhead reintroduce N-dependence at moderate sizes before the asymptotic O(lmax) kicks in?
basis: Fig. 5 and the modularisation argument were only confirmed structurally at N=6 in this replication. The claim 'system-size-independent depth ~lmax' is asymptotic; for N in the 8-15 range (where NISQ hardware actually lives), the overhead of covering all C(N,2) couplings with modules of size lmax may still grow noticeably. This matters for any real hardware roadmap.
next_steps: Extend the driver-line generator to N in {8, 10, 12, 15} (Hilbert space up to 2^{29} which needs sparse-Hamiltonian evolution, not full statevector). For each N, generate the modularised implicit driver with lmax fixed at 5, count (a) number of driver lines, (b) max line length, (c) total two-qubit-gate depth per QAOA layer after a naive linear-nearest-neighbor compilation. Plot depth vs N and check whether depth is genuinely flat (as claimed) or grows sub-linearly / linearly with a small prefactor. Compare against a standard-QAOA compiled to the same LHZ grid. Free endpoint: local CPU with scipy.sparse Krylov evolution, no accelerator required; ~4 CPU-hours.
